units.text: We'll follow a S Q L query without starting a warehouse cluster. Athena uses the catalog to interpret the files, then reads the selected data from S three. The catalog describes the objects; it doesn't hold the data rows.

Use the workgroup to separate settings and controls. Check permission to read the input and write the result location. Verify that query results reach the configured S three location when using customer-managed query results.
Compare reading raw files with reading selected columns from Parquet. Then filter on a real partition so Athena skips unrelated files. The same result can require fewer scanned bytes.
Check the query's reported bytes scanned, not just elapsed time. Columnar format, sensible compression and suitable file sizes can help, but verify the gain with the workload you actually run.

Federation lets Athena query supported remote data without first moving the entire source into S three. In this example a Lambda-based connector reads the remote source and returns data that Athena can combine with lake data.

Check the connector's access to its source and any configured S three spill location. Apply filters so it doesn't pull back unnecessary data. It still does remote work, so measure source load and access separately from the Athena result.
We'll turn governed data into a dashboard a reader can use. Start with a dataset, build an analysis, then publish the dashboard. The published view is not a shared editing copy of the analysis.
Sharing gives readers access to the intended artifact. Dataset security can still restrict which rows they see. Verify the experience as a reader, not only as the author.
Direct query depends on the source at query time. SPICE imports data, so a dashboard can respond without asking the source for every interaction. The trade-off is that the import must stay current.
Choose a refresh schedule that matches how old the data can be. Test the last successful refresh and verify a known new record appears. Fast load time doesn't tell you how current the dashboard is.
The author prepares a dataset and builds an analysis. Publishing makes a dashboard readers can consume. Grant access to the intended people or groups without granting editing rights by default.
Dashboard permissions decide who can open it; data rules decide what they can see. Verify both with an intended reader and someone who shouldn't have the same data access.

We'll choose a service for each job in a lake architecture. Keep durable data in S three, then choose Glue for suitable managed transformations or E M R when the workload needs the processing engines and controls it provides.

Athena can query lake files in place. Redshift is a warehouse option when sustained analytical workloads call for it. A dashboard consumes that result; it doesn't replace the processing, catalog or query layer beneath it.
Device telemetry arrives in Data Streams. A reader can track its position and replay retained events. Firehose delivers a copy to S three, which is where the lake query can find the landed objects.

Athena queries the stored data, then the dashboard presents it. If a reading isn't visible, check the stream, delivered file, catalog and dashboard refresh in order. Each stage can be healthy while the next is delayed.

Use E M R for a distributed processing engine, Athena to query existing lake data without managing a warehouse, and Redshift for warehouse workloads. The question is what work the engine needs to do, not whether all three can run S Q L in some form.

Look at the shape of a representative query, where the data already lives and the operating effort. A one-off read and a heavily used shared reporting model can need different services even when both start with S three data.

We'll trace a test record from the stream to a S Q L result. Send one recognizable event through Data Streams, then check that Firehose lands the expected record in S three. Successful ingestion isn't proof the file arrived.

The catalog gives Athena the shape and location to query. Find the test record in the result. For a controlled invalid-record test, verify rejected records land in the configured failure path rather than silently disappearing.
Watch the job position: Batch has accepted it, but runnable means the container hasn't started yet. Debug compute placement before looking for runtime code errors.
Check queue association, eligible compute, resource requests and reported reasons. Change the constraint that actually prevents placement. Then verify the job runs and the expected output exists.
Catalog the raw files, then organize suitable data as partitioned Parquet to reduce scans. Compare the same query over the two layouts so a change in scanned bytes has a clear cause.

Publish the intended result as a dashboard and test with an authorized reader. Confirm both freshness and data access. A new dashboard doesn't automatically refresh its source or make every record appropriate to share.

Build a baseline query result, create the encrypted recovery point, and verify the copy reached its destination with the needed key access. That gives you something restorable, not a live standby endpoint.

Restore to the supported target, then check client access plus warehouse and external lake queries. The restored warehouse and connection need validation; do not stop the recovery clock merely because restore finished.

We'll choose the security tool by asking what we need to know. CloudTrail can help explain A P I activity. Config can help explain configuration change. For this walkthrough, our question is which supported resources have known software exposure, so we'll follow Inspector.

Inspector can assess supported E C two instances, container images and Lambda functions according to their scan types. First confirm activation and coverage. An empty list does not tell you that an unsupported or inactive resource is clean.

Use findings to prioritize remediation. Fix the package, artifact, or configuration the finding actually concerns. Then verify rescanning observed the remediated deployment; suppressing the alert isn't fixing the issue.

Walk through activation, supported resource type and prerequisites before looking at findings. A resource that wasn't scanned may not have findings at all. Confirm that it was covered during the review window.

Findings describe what the supported scans detected. Use reporting integrations if configured, but retain the coverage check. A centralized dashboard showing zero findings doesn't prove every account and Region was assessed.

The agent-based route uses Systems Manager on eligible instances. In hybrid mode, eligible instances that aren't agent managed can be assessed through the agentless E B S snapshot path. Check prerequisites to distinguish excluded instances from assessed instances.
Network reachability is separate from package scanning. Use its evidence to understand exposure, not as proof that the package version is vulnerable or clean.

The container finding belongs to the scanned image digest. Rebuild the image with a fixed dependency and verify the corrected artifact is actually deployed. Pushing a new tag by itself doesn't update what is running.

For Lambda, check which function artifact was assessed and which scanning features are active. Package scans and eligible optional code scanning are distinct. Deploy the fix and verify Inspector's updated finding or coverage for the intended function.

Rank findings by severity and the resource's actual exposure, then assign the owner to fix the underlying package or image. Redeploy and let Inspector reassess. Verify the finding status rather than treating a ticket closure as evidence.

In the example the owner rebuilds the container with a corrected dependency, pushes the new artifact, and deploys it. Confirm the running digest matches the fixed one, then verify the old finding was addressed in the workload.
